raw_findings.message: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which are cheap to crack offline, especially because the hashes are exposed by the profile endpoint.
The reader accounts use a fixed compiled-in password, and the admin password is also hard-coded in `main.go`, so anyone who obtains the source can log in with these credentials.
`windowStarted` is never initialized, so it remains zero and the window is reset on every attempt, allowing unlimited login guesses.
A login for an unknown username makes `account` nil and panics when its password hash is accessed.
Session tokens are derived from the current timestamp rather than generated randomly, allowing an attacker to guess tokens and impersonate users.
Every successful login adds a session that is never expired or removed, so repeated logins can grow the in-memory map until the service runs out of memory.
The unvalidated `next` parameter is passed to `http.Redirect`, allowing a successful login to redirect users to an attacker-controlled site.
Any authenticated user can select any account by query parameter and retrieve its profile, including an admin's details.
The profile response exposes password hashes to every authenticated caller, enabling offline cracking of account passwords.
An authenticated caller controls the URL fetched by the server and can use the proxy to access internal or otherwise restricted services.
The request uses the default HTTP client with no timeout, so an authenticated caller can target a server that stalls and tie up handler goroutines and connections indefinitely.
The unauthenticated health endpoint returns the signing key, exposing a value intended to be secret to any caller.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The application seeds accounts with the publicly known password `bluebird42`, allowing anyone who knows this default to authenticate as either reader.
The login handler decodes an unbounded request body, so a client can send an enormous password or username to consume memory and CPU.
Successful logins create sessions with no expiration or cleanup, so stolen tokens remain valid until rotation and repeated logins can grow the session map indefinitely.
When `next` is supplied, the handler redirects without returning the newly created bearer token or setting a session cookie, leaving the client unable to use that session.
The proxy blocks special-purpose IPv4 prefixes but not reserved IPv6 ranges such as `2001:db8::/32`, which `IsGlobalUnicast` accepts and the proxy may connect to if such a range is routed internally.

raw_findings.message: Because `windowStarted` is never initialized or updated, this condition resets the attempt count on every request and allows unlimited login attempts.
Passwords are hashed with fast, unsalted SHA-1, allowing captured hashes to be cracked efficiently offline.
An unauthenticated request with an unknown username makes `account` nil and panics when its password hash is accessed.
Session tokens are derived from the current timestamp rather than cryptographically secure randomness, allowing attackers to predict or guess valid tokens.
After a successful login, an attacker-controlled `next` URL can redirect the user to an external site for phishing.
The profile response exposes each account's password hash to any authenticated caller, enabling offline password cracking.
An authenticated caller can make the server issue HTTP requests to arbitrary `target` URLs, including internal services.
The unauthenticated health endpoint returns the signing key, exposing a purported secret to anyone who can reach the service.
The administrator password is embedded in source code, so anyone who obtains the source or binary can authenticate as admin.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The seeded reader accounts use the fixed password `bluebird42`, so anyone who can reach the login endpoint can authenticate as Alice or Bob with credentials disclosed in the source.
The login handler decodes an unlimited request body, allowing an attacker to send a very large JSON password and exhaust memory or processing resources.
Issued bearer tokens are stored without an expiry or removal path, so a stolen token remains valid indefinitely until an administrator rotates sessions.

The address check treats IPv6 NAT64 addresses such as `64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe` as public, so on a network with NAT64 routing a caller can reach the translated private IPv4 address.

raw_findings.message: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which can be cracked quickly if an attacker obtains the hashes.
windowStarted is never initialized or updated, so the zero time makes this condition reset the counter on every attempt and leaves password guessing unrestricted.
The unauthenticated login handler decodes an unrestricted request body, so a client can submit an enormous password field and consume excessive server memory.
An unknown username makes account nil, and the subsequent password-hash dereference panics for every such login request.
Session tokens are Unix timestamps rather than cryptographically random values, so an attacker who can estimate the login time can guess valid bearer tokens.
Sessions are stored without expiration or revocation, so a stolen token remains valid for the lifetime of the process.
The caller-controlled next URL is accepted without validation, allowing a logged-in user to be redirected to an attacker-controlled site.
Any authenticated user can retrieve every account's password hash, enabling offline cracking of other users' credentials.
An authenticated user can make the server fetch an arbitrary target URL, including internal services and loopback addresses.
The unauthenticated health endpoint returns the signing key, exposing it to any caller.
The administrator password is a fixed source-code literal, allowing anyone who obtains the deployed credentials or source to log in as admin.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The seeded alice and bob accounts always use the publicly known password `bluebird42`, so anyone who can reach the login endpoint can authenticate as either user.
The login handler decodes an unbounded request body, allowing an unauthenticated client to send a huge JSON password and consume excessive memory and CPU during parsing and password hashing.
Sessions are stored without an expiration time or per-session revocation, so a stolen bearer token remains valid indefinitely unless an administrator rotates all sessions.

The handler stores a session before validating `next` and never returns the token or sets a cookie on the redirect path, so repeated login requests with `next` create inaccessible session entries and can grow the session map without bound.
